title: Speak to him gently
hookLine: Allah sends Musa and Harun to Pharaoh and tells them to speak gently

lines: THE WORST MAN IN THE STORY.
cards: You know the fantasy. The person who hurt you, the impossible boss, the relative who says the worst thing at every holiday, and you finally get your moment. You've rehearsed it in the shower a hundred times.
Now take the worst person in the Qur'an. Pharaoh. He killed babies.
He called himself a god. He enslaved a whole people. Musa and Harun are about to walk into his court with the backing of the Lord of the worlds.
If anyone ever had permission to let someone have it, surely it's now. Then they get their instructions.

teach.b: Surah Ta-Ha. Go, you and your brother, with My signs, and don't grow slack in remembering Me. Go, both of you, to Pharaoh.

teach.h: SPEAK TO HIM A GENTLE WORD.
teach.b: And speak to him a gentle word, that perhaps he may take heed, or feel some fear. The Arabic is qawlan layyinan: a soft word, a pliable word, the kind that bends instead of breaks.
The command doesn't pretend Pharaoh is a good man. And still: gently.
The verse gives the reason: perhaps he may take heed. Gentleness leaves a door open. A shout closes it.

Muslim teachers have drawn a lesson from this for centuries, and it's often repeated: if Musa, one of the greatest prophets, was told to speak gently to Pharaoh, one of the worst of men, then how should we speak to each other, none of us as good as Musa, and none of those we argue with as bad as Pharaoh?
Then Musa and Harun say what anyone would: our Lord, we're afraid he'll rush at us, or go too far. And the answer: don't be afraid.
I am with you both. I hear, and I see.
So the gentleness isn't weakness. They aren't soft because they're scared. They've been told they're not alone, and that frees them to be kind to a tyrant.

The Prophet Muhammad ﷺ said something that fits right alongside: in a hadith in Sahih Muslim, he said gentleness is never in a thing without making it beautiful, and never taken from a thing without making it ugly.

how: Muslim teachers often cite the command to speak gently to Pharaoh (Qur'an 20:44) as the model for how to speak to anyone, especially in disagreement or when inviting others to faith.

games.q: what's inside the story — tap the pairs.

s: Musa was told to speak harshly to Pharaoh because he was a tyrant
he was told to speak to him a gentle word, perhaps he'd take heed.
the command to be gentle says Pharaoh was a good man
it says outright he has transgressed all bounds, and still: gently.
Musa and Harun admitted they were afraid
they said he might rush at them, and were told: don't be afraid, I am with you both.

games.q: you're Musa, sent to Pharaoh, a man who killed babies and called himself a god. how are you told to speak to him?
o: with a warning of the punishment coming.
with a gentle word, that perhaps he may take heed.
say nothing. let the signs speak.
games.why: speak to him a gentle word, that perhaps he may take heed or fear. gentleness leaves a door open, even for Pharaoh.

practice: Bring to mind someone you find hard, a medium one, not the hardest, and a true sentence you'd like to say to them, the one with some edge on it.

Without making it false, soften it: take out the word that stings, add their name, leave a door open at the end, and say it quietly until it sounds like you. If you pray, you can ask for a gentle word.

wordCard.voice: Qawlan layyinan, a gentle word: what Musa and Harun were told to speak even to Pharaoh, so a door might stay open.

orig.note: Arabic, from Qur'an 20:44: "a gentle word" — soft, pliable speech.

carryVoice: Your line: gently, even to pharaoh. Gentle, and not afraid of him. Tomorrow, the magicians.

sources.ref: Sahih Muslim 2594 (gentleness is not in anything except that it beautifies it)
